title: Guide Student Practice: Rosenshine's Principles of Instruction [FREE GUIDE & RESOURCE]
author: Jamie Lee Clark
summary: Clark presents Rosenshine's principle of guided practice, the We Do phase between teacher modelling and independent work. He argues that new learning is fragile and is forgotten or mis-encoded without enough supported rehearsal. Quoting Rosenshine, he explains that effective teachers spend more time on guided practice, combining short explanations with supervised work until success rates reach about eighty percent. He gives implementation advice: co-work the first steps, have students teach steps back, coach while circulating, keep rehearsal targeted and vary the format. The newsletter ends by pointing to a lesson-planner download and paid resources.
points: Guided practice is scaffolded rehearsal in which the teacher stays with the class, prompting, questioning and correcting.
Immediate feedback during rehearsal stops errors becoming habits.
Effective teachers spend notably more time on guided practice than less effective teachers.
Short targeted bursts of rehearsal beat long unfocused work time.
Varying the format, such as co-working, teach-back, quick drills and error-spotting, keeps guided practice fresh.
quotes: Instead of moving straight from demonstration to “off you go,” it’s about staying with the class, prompting, questioning, and correcting as students practise new material in small steps.

Successful teachers spend more time guiding students’ practice of new material… It is not enough simply to present students with new material, because the material will be forgotten unless there is sufficient rehearsal.
Research in cognitive science shows that new learning is fragile, ephemeral and can easily be forgotten. Without enough rehearsal, students quickly forget or encode misconceptions.
Feedback prevents misconceptions: Immediate correction stops errors from becoming habits (practice can be a disaster if students are practising errors).

Studies of effective teachers show they spend significantly more time on guided practice than less effective teachers, combining short explanations with supervised student work until success rates hit ~80%.
